title: ACCTG 211H Companion
text:
Welcome
This is the ACCTG 211H Companion, the textbook for Honors Financial and Managerial Accounting for Decision Making at Penn State. It asks: What would someone need to know to entrust resources to an organization, and what can its accounts actually tell them?
You do not need to plan a career in accounting to use these ideas. They help you evaluate an employer, understand a business proposal, question a performance measure, or assess a claim about an organization’s finances.

section: Begin with the opening unit
text:
Begin with the opening unit
The first five weeks develop a sequence of increasingly realistic settings:

Information and cooperation: why records and credible reports matter.
Certainty: value, income, distributions, and linked statements when future cash flows are known.
Uncertainty: expected income, news, and revisions to value.
Information and incentives: learning from reports and evaluating performance.
The framework and first accrual statements: recognition, measurement, disclosure, and transaction analysis.

One small model enterprise connects the numerical examples. A separate, fully specified Campus Curb operating case then introduces GAAP accounting. Each case states its assumptions; do not mix their numbers.

title: Preface: Reading, Practice, and Evidence
text:
The four arcs
Arc I — Information, Value, and Reporting (Chapters 1–5). Begin with the demand for information. Build accounting under certainty, introduce shared uncertainty, then introduce imperfect reports and incentives. The FASB framework and first systematic GAAP entries follow those economic questions.
Arc II — Markets and Measurement (Chapters 6–10). Examine how users interpret earnings and cash flows, how assets and liabilities are measured, and how compensation interacts with reporting. Value and income are related, but they are not interchangeable.
Arc III — Contracting and Internal Information (Chapters 11–13). Apply the same ideas to cost behavior, performance measures, decentralization, and investment decisions inside an organization.
Arc IV — Synthesis (Chapter 14). Use the concepts and evidence to evaluate contested reporting choices. A defensible answer identifies its assumptions and explains what evidence would change it.

section: Three distinct kinds of number
text:
Three distinct kinds of number
Cash flow records a receipt or payment. Accounting income reports performance under a recognition and measurement system. Value depends on prospective benefits and the valuation assumptions. A change in any one does not automatically imply an equal change in the others.
The opening examples intentionally simplify firms so you can trace these connections. They identify when a calculation is a model benchmark, a proposed policy, or the supplied accounting treatment for a transaction. Keep those settings separate.

text:
Read research as an argument supported by evidence
For an empirical study, identify the question, sample, measure, comparison, main result, and limitation. Ask whether the evidence supports association or a causal inference. For a theory paper, identify the assumptions, mechanism, and prediction. A numerical classroom example illustrates a mechanism; it does not establish that the mechanism dominates in actual firms.
A result that differs from your prediction is an opportunity to investigate data, design, or assumptions. It is not a reason to alter an analysis until it produces the expected picture.

title: 1  Why Accounting? Information and Cooperation
text:
1.1 Would you entrust your money to Campus Curb?
Three students want to expand Campus Curb, a hypothetical campus delivery service. They ask you to invest. They know their delivery routes, repeat customers, damaged scooters, and unpaid bills. You have a pitch deck and a promise that the business is doing well.
You might ask how much cash it has. You might ask whether customers have paid, whether the scooters need replacing, or whether the founders owe their couriers wages. You might also ask how the founders will pay themselves. A business can have cash because it borrowed yesterday; it can have satisfied customers and still struggle to pay its bills. A confident founder can be either well informed or overconfident.
These questions arise before anyone mentions an accounting standard. People need information when they entrust resources to others. Resources include an investor’s money, a supplier’s goods delivered on credit, a courier’s work before payday, or a donor’s contribution to a campus nonprofit. Each person wants to know something about what has happened and what may happen next.
Accounting creates organized records and reports about an entity’s resources, obligations, and activities. It can help people decide whether to cooperate, evaluate what happened after they cooperated, and hold someone accountable. It cannot eliminate every uncertainty or make conflicting interests disappear.
Our guiding question is: What would someone need to know to entrust resources to this organization, and what can its accounts actually tell them?

section: 1.2 Three different reasons you might not know
text:
1.2 Three different reasons you might not know
Different problems require different responses. We need more precise language than simply calling everything an information problem.









Situation
What is unknown, and to whom?
Main problem




An unexpected storm may interrupt deliveries. Neither founders nor investors know whether it will occur.
Everyone faces the same unknown future event.
Shared uncertainty


A founder knows that half the scooters have damaged batteries but does not tell a prospective investor.
One party already knows a relevant fact the other lacks.
Information asymmetry: hidden information


After receiving investment, a founder can skip maintenance, and investors cannot observe that choice directly.
One party cannot observe another’s action.
Information asymmetry: hidden action




Adverse selection arises when hidden information affects who is willing to enter a transaction or which terms they accept. Moral hazard arises when imperfectly observed actions affect the outcome of a relationship. These labels describe features of an economic arrangement; they do not require an assumption that everyone is dishonest.
A founder may honestly know more about scooter condition than an investor. A capable employee may reasonably dislike a compensation plan that makes pay depend on weather. Reporting and contracts must work in settings containing honest mistakes, ordinary uncertainty, and conflicting incentives as well as deliberate deception.






Try the distinction



A nonprofit director and a donor both know that next month’s fundraising revenue could be high or low. That is shared uncertainty. If the director privately knows that a major donor has withdrawn, information is asymmetric. If the director later reduces fundraising effort without the donor being able to observe it, the problem involves hidden action.

title: 1  Why Accounting? Information and Cooperation
section: 1.3 Why hidden information can prevent useful trade
text:
1.3 Why hidden information can prevent useful trade
Suppose students are selling used scooters. Half are reliable and half need repairs. A buyer values a reliable scooter at $1,200 and a repair-prone scooter at $600. A reliable scooter’s owner will sell for at least $1,000; a repair-prone scooter’s owner will sell for at least $400.
If condition is observable, both kinds can trade. A reliable scooter can sell between $1,000 and $1,200, making both parties better off. A repair-prone scooter can sell between $400 and $600. For each scooter, the buyer values it more than its current owner does.
Now suppose sellers know condition but buyers cannot tell the difference. If both types were offered, the buyer’s average valuation would be
\[
0.5(1{,}200)+0.5(600)=900.
\]
But $900 is below the reliable owner’s minimum price. Reliable owners withdraw. Buyers must revise their beliefs about the scooters still offered: the original half-and-half composition no longer describes the market. If only repair-prone scooters remain, a buyer values a scooter at $600.
The result is a market in repair-prone scooters, with reliable scooters excluded despite the potential gains from trading them. This is adverse selection: the price offered to a mixed pool changes who remains in it. The logic follows the problem made famous by Akerlof (1970). Our example loses some beneficial trade; it does not predict that every market with asymmetric information completely collapses.
An average price is not automatically an equilibrium price. Ask: Who would accept it? Given those participants, what would buyers pay? Beliefs about quality and participation must be consistent.

Would an inspection help?
Suppose a trusted inspector can perfectly verify condition for $50, paid by the seller. A reliable scooter sold for $1,100 leaves the seller $1,050 after inspection, exceeding the seller’s $1,000 minimum, while the buyer receives something worth $1,200. Inspection can restore that trade.
The assumptions matter: the inspection is accurate, buyers trust it, the result cannot be forged, and the fee is small enough relative to the gains from trade. An inspection costing $250 would exceed the $200 total gains available from trading this reliable scooter.
Other arrangements can help: warranties, repeated dealings, reputation, legal remedies, or a seller retaining exposure to future failures. Each has costs and limitations. Accounting and auditing belong to this larger family of institutions that help people transact despite unequal information.

section: 1.4 From scooters to financial reports
text:
1.4 From scooters to financial reports
Campus Curb’s founders are offering claims on a business rather than selling individual scooters. The information gap is more complicated, but a similar problem remains. If outsiders cannot distinguish an attractive opportunity from a weak one, they may offer terms that attractive firms refuse. Useful projects may fail to attract resources.
A report organizes answers to recurring questions:









Report
Basic question
Campus Curb example




Balance sheet
What resources and obligations exist at a date?
Cash, equipment, unpaid wages, and borrowing.


Income statement
What performance is reported over a period?
Delivery revenue and operating expenses.


Statement of cash flows
Where did cash come from, and where did it go?
Customer receipts, equipment purchases, and borrowing.


Statement of changes in equity
Why did owners’ recorded claims change?
Contributions, income or loss, and distributions.


Notes
What do the numbers mean, and what qualifications matter?
Methods, commitments, and uncertainty.




For now, learn the questions rather than detailed formats. The next chapter builds small, complete statements in a world simple enough to check every number.
The accounting equation is
\[
\text{Assets}=\text{Liabilities}+\text{Equity}.
\tag{1.1}\]
Assets are the entity’s resources as recognized and measured in its accounts; liabilities are its recognized obligations; equity is the residual. If recognized assets are $8,000 and liabilities are $3,000, equity is $5,000. “Recognized” matters: a reported amount is included in statements under a measurement convention, not automatically the market value of everything that makes a business valuable.

A balanced report can still be false
Suppose Campus Curb invents $1,000 of delivery revenue and a corresponding customer receivable. Reported assets increase by $1,000; the fictitious income increases equity by $1,000. The equation still balances.
Double entry imposes a useful consistency discipline, but balancing does not establish that a delivery occurred or that a customer owes money. Credibility also depends on evidence, appropriate measurement, controls, and independent scrutiny. A customer confirmation or delivery record addresses a question arithmetic alone cannot answer.
An audit provides independent assurance about financial statements; it is not a guarantee that a company will succeed or that every error has been found. Keep a report’s credibility separate from the attractiveness of the opportunity it describes. A credible report can reveal an unattractive business.

title: 1  Why Accounting? Information and Cooperation
section: 1.5 Records help people cooperate and remember
text:
1.5 Records help people cooperate and remember
Financial reporting is not useful only because public-company shareholders cannot watch managers. Consider a student organization selling tickets for a concert. Even if all officers are honest and share the same information today, records help them remember which vendors have been paid, which tickets have been sold, and what the next group of officers will inherit.
The separation of ownership and control adds another reason for reporting. Someone supplies resources while another person chooses how to use them. Berle and Means (1932) and Jensen and Meckling (1976) provide influential accounts of this relationship. We return to incentives in Chapter 4. You do not need their full models to recognize the problem: an outcome such as profit combines decisions, circumstances, and luck.
Reports can support decision making—choosing what to do—and stewardship—evaluating how entrusted resources have been used. They can also improve coordination between people without an agency conflict. No single story exhausts accounting’s uses.

section: 1.6 Research brief: does access to records change exchange?
text:
1.6 Research brief: does access to records change exchange?
Basu et al. (2009) study recordkeeping in a laboratory exchange setting. They compare economies with and without recordkeeping and find that records support reciprocity, reputation formation, and coordination. This is evidence about a mechanism through which records can affect cooperation, rather than simply describe it.
For the assigned excerpt, identify the treatment and comparison, choose one reported result, and explain why the experimental setting helps evaluate the mechanism. Identify one reason it might not transfer unchanged to a modern firm. Experimental evidence about exchange does not, by itself, establish an account of ancient economic development.
Your task is to interpret the comparison, not reproduce the statistical analysis. The classroom games are illustrations rather than replications of this study.

section: 1.8 Optional extension: where the economic theories fit
text:
1.8 Optional extension: where the economic theories fit
Akerlof asks how hidden information affects exchange. Coase asks why some activities are coordinated inside firms rather than through markets (Coase 1937). Jensen and Meckling examine costs arising when decision authority is delegated (Jensen and Meckling 1976). Basu and Waymire consider the broader role of recordkeeping in cooperation (Basu and Waymire 2006).
Choose one theory and connect its question to an organization you know. Describe what it helps explain and one feature it leaves out. A model clarifies a mechanism under assumptions; it need not be a complete history or justification of accounting practice.
Next we temporarily remove the information problems. That gives us a benchmark against which to understand what uncertainty and imperfect reporting change.

title: 2  Value and Income Under Certainty
text:
2.1 Remove one difficulty before adding another
What would valuation and accounting look like if everyone knew future cash flows and the interest rate? For this chapter, assume there are no taxes or transaction costs and investors can borrow or lend at the same rate. Our small enterprise is financed entirely by owners. These are model assumptions, not descriptions of real businesses or requirements of GAAP.
A number can change because time passes, even when nobody learns anything. Income can be positive without being surprising. Cash can be received without all of it being income. Scott develops this ideal-conditions approach (Scott and O’Brien 2020, chap. 2); the numerical cases here are teaching examples.

section: 2.2 A payment in the future
text:
2.2 A payment in the future
Calculator warm-up. A 10% annual return turns 100 into 100 × 1.10 = 110 after one year and 110 × 1.10 = 121 after two. To work backward from 121, divide by 1.10 twice. Writing \((1.10)^2\) means \(1.10\times1.10\), not \(1.10\times2\). Always count the years between the valuation date and the payment date.
Suppose an investment pays $1,000 exactly two years from now. The annual interest rate is 5%. Investing $100 today gives you $105 after one year and $110.25 after two. Interest in the second year is earned on the accumulated amount.
Work backward to find the amount today that grows to $1,000:
\[
PV_0=\frac{1{,}000}{(1.05)^2}=907.03.
\]
Present value is the value at a specified date of a future cash flow, calculated using a discount rate. The subscript 0 identifies today. One year from now the claim is worth
\[
PV_1=\frac{1{,}000}{1.05}=952.38.
\]

The claim gains $45.35 in Year 1 without a cash receipt. That is accretion of the discount: the payment is one year closer. It equals 5% of opening value, subject to rounding. At maturity, the $1,000 receipt includes recovery of the investment, not just the final year’s income.
Why is present value the price in this model? If an identical certain payment could be obtained more cheaply by lending, buyers would choose lending. If the claim offered a better return than the borrowing cost, investors could borrow to acquire it. Under our trading assumptions, those opportunities prevent different prices for identical payments. This is a no-arbitrage argument; it depends on the relevant trades being possible.

title: 2  Value and Income Under Certainty
section: 2.4 The first year: cash, income, and capital recovery
text:
2.4 The first year: cash, income, and capital recovery
At the end of Year 1, only the second $660 receipt remains. Its present value is $600. The delivery asset’s value falls from $1,145.45 to $600 as the first year’s services are used.
Economic depreciation is this decline in the productive asset’s value in our certainty example:
\[
1{,}145.45-600=545.45.
\]
Economic income is net cash generated less the reduction in asset value:
\[
I_1=660-545.45=114.55.
\]
Equivalently, the owner’s economic income is the distribution plus the change in the remaining investment’s value:
\[
I_1=D_1+V_1-V_0=660+600-1{,}145.45=114.55.
\tag{2.2}\]
Here \(D_t\) is the distribution and \(V_t\) is enterprise value after that distribution. There are no new contributions in this formula. A contribution must be excluded from income, just as we excluded the initial contribution.
Keep dates and periods separate. Asset value and equity describe what remains at a date; receipts, distributions, and income describe what happens during a period. In this all-equity model, enterprise value equals the value of all remaining assets, including any retained cash. It equals the delivery asset alone only when there is no other asset. We are using present values here; a later accounting carrying amount need not equal economic value.
Of the $660 received, $114.55 is a return on the investment and the remainder is capital recovery. Income is also 10% of opening value: $1,145.45 × 10% = $114.55.






A distribution is not an expense



Generating income and distributing cash are different events. If the enterprise instead kept the $660 at year-end, it would have $660 cash plus the $600 asset. Total value would be $1,260, with the same $114.55 income. A distribution reduces cash and equity; it does not reduce income.


Try a partial distribution. Suppose Campus Curb distributes only $400 of Year 1’s receipt and keeps the rest as cash at the reporting instant. Find closing cash, total assets, equity, and income before opening the answer. Everything else is unchanged.






Check the partial-distribution case





Cash is $260. The delivery asset is still worth $600, so total assets and equity are $860. Income is $400 + $860 − $1,145.45 = $114.55. Counting the full receipt as a distribution would count the retained $260 twice. Changing the payout alone has not changed this year’s income; future returns on retained cash are outside this reporting instant.

2.10 Optional extension: residual income
If owners require return \(r\) on beginning book equity \(B_{t-1}\), define residual income as accounting income after a charge for capital:
\[
RI_t=NI_t-rB_{t-1}.
\]

3.1 An uncertain outcome need not be private information
Campus Curb’s founders and investors might agree on the possible outcomes and their probabilities without knowing which will occur. This is uncertainty with symmetric information. It is different from a manager concealing a fact already known to her.
In this chapter, everyone shares the same probability model. Investors are risk neutral: for the payoffs considered here they value an uncertain dollar amount at its expected amount before discounting for time. They can borrow and lend at the stated interest rate, and we retain the other simplifying assumptions from Chapter 2. These assumptions let us introduce uncertainty without simultaneously introducing a pricing model for risk or a credibility problem.
Risk neutrality is a teaching assumption. It does not mean that real investors are indifferent to all risks or that a risky investment should always be discounted at the risk-free rate.

text:
3.2 An expected value is a weighted average
Suppose a claim pays $880 in a high-demand state and $440 in a low-demand state. Each state has probability 0.5. Its expected payoff is
\[
E[X]=0.5(880)+0.5(440)=660.
\]
The weights sum to one. They describe our uncertainty, not a promise to receive part of each outcome. The actual receipt will be $880 or $440; it will never be $660 in this example. An expectation can be useful even though it is not a possible realization.
A report that estimates $660 has not necessarily made an error when the outcome is $440. To judge the estimate, ask what information was available when it was made, whether the probability model was appropriate, and whether that model was applied honestly and correctly. A single unfavorable outcome cannot answer all those questions.

3.7 A useful report can deliver bad news
In the low state, disclosing the news reduces the remaining asset’s value from its prior expectation of $600 to $400. The report has not destroyed a $200 physical resource. It has changed what users know about an already-existing economic situation.
That distinction matters when interpreting evidence. A negative price response does not establish that disclosure was socially harmful. Conversely, an announcement followed by a price increase does not prove that the reporting rule created wealth. Users may simply have learned good news.
The question becomes sharper when users must choose an action. Would a lender offer the same amount after learning the low state? Would a prospective investor buy at the seller’s proposed price? In the next chapter we make the report imperfect and ask how much a decision maker would pay for it.

section: 4.3 How much is information worth for a decision?
text:
4.3 How much is information worth for a decision?
Consider a separate prospective investment decision at the end of Year 1. An investor can pay $700 now for a claim to the same kind of Year 2 payoff. The investor has not bought it yet and can decline. This choice is distinct from valuing the claim already owned by the model enterprise.
Without a report, the claim is worth $600, so the investor declines. With the noisy report, she buys only after a favorable result: $720 value minus $700 price gives $20 of expected net benefit. A favorable report occurs with probability 0.5, so the expected benefit of having the report before paying its fee is $10. An $8 fee paid at that decision date leaves $2 net benefit.
With perfect information she would buy only in the high state, when value is $800. The expected benefit would be 0.5($800 − $700) = $50. This is an upper comparison for the information choices in this particular decision, not a general market price for perfect information.
Notice why the report helps: the investor changes her action. More precise information need not change every decision. If the price were low enough that she would buy after either report, this report would have no gross decision value in the simplified setting, even though it changes her valuation.

title: 4  Information, Credibility, and Incentives
section: 4.4 Who produces the report, and why believe it?
text:
4.4 Who produces the report, and why believe it?
So far the diagnostic arrives automatically with known error rates. Real reports are produced by people. Suppose the founders observe the diagnostic privately. Outsiders now face an information asymmetry, and the founders may prefer a favorable interpretation.
Several mechanisms need to be distinguished:









Mechanism
What carries information?
Example




Routine accounting recognition
A transaction, obligation, or use of resources
Interest accumulated under a known loan contract.


Estimation
A model applied to incomplete evidence
An estimate of uncollectible customer balances.


Verifiable disclosure
Truthful evidence that can be checked if released
A signed customer contract shown to an investor.


Costly signaling
An observable action that different types have different incentives to take
A warranty that is more expensive for sellers of unreliable scooters.


Misstatement
A depiction inconsistent with the relevant facts or requirements
Omitting interest merely because no bill has arrived.




A useful number need not be a costly signal. A cost by itself does not make a statement true. Equally, an estimate that later differs from the realization need not have been a misstatement.

Why silence can be informative
If an informed seller can disclose a value truthfully, verifiably, and without cost, favorable types want to distinguish themselves from less favorable ones. As they disclose, the remaining silent pool becomes less attractive. This is the intuition behind disclosure unraveling (Grossman 1981; Milgrom 1981).
Real disclosure can be incomplete because releasing information has costs or because investors do not know whether a manager possesses information (Verrecchia 1983; Dye 1985). Silence can then reflect bad news, proprietary concerns, or a lack of information. It should not automatically be read as proof of fraud or as proof that the firm is the worst type.


What makes a reporting process credible?
For Campus Curb, compare the founders’ unsupported sales forecast with a report that identifies the underlying orders, distinguishes cancellable orders, explains collection assumptions, and is checked by an independent party. The latter gives users more ways to evaluate the claim.
Internal controls can separate authorization, custody, and recordkeeping; reconciliations can expose differences; outside confirmation can test whether a balance exists. These mechanisms have costs and do not remove all judgment. Their purpose is to make relevant claims more dependable and errors more likely to be detected.

4.8 Optional extension: a costly signal is not a free improvement
In a stripped-down Spence example (Spence 1973), high-productivity workers produce 100 and low-productivity workers 60. Education \(e\) costs a high type \(e\) and a low type \(2e\) and does not itself raise productivity. Employers pay 100 above threshold \(e^*\) and 60 otherwise.
Separation requires \(100-e^*\ge60\) and \(60\ge100-2e^*\), giving \(20\le e^*\le40\). At 20, high types net 80 and low types net 60; low types are indifferent about mimicking, so the threshold case needs the corresponding tie-breaking behavior.
If the high-type share is \(\lambda\), the no-signal pooling wage is \(60+40\lambda\). Low types lose from separation for every positive \(\lambda\); high types gain only when \(\lambda<0.5\). The signal can sort types while using resources and redistributing pay. It is not automatically a Pareto improvement.

section: 4.9 Optional extension: the LEN model
text:
4.9 Optional extension: the LEN model
Suppose output is \(y=e+\varepsilon\) with normally distributed noise of variance \(\sigma^2\), effort cost \(ke^2/2\), a risk-neutral principal, and an agent with exponential utility and absolute risk aversion \(a>0\). Restrict compensation to \(w=b+\beta y\) and choose the fixed payment to satisfy participation. The agent’s certainty equivalent is
\[
CE=b+\beta e-\frac{ke^2}{2}-\frac{a\beta^2\sigma^2}{2}.
\]
Optimal effort is \(e=\beta/k\). Within this linear-contract setup the optimal slope is \(\beta^*=1/(1+ak\sigma^2)\). Greater noise or risk aversion weakens incentives because performance pay imposes risk. This is a separate risk-averse extension of the simple classroom contract, not an assumption needed for the main text.

title: 5  From Economic Questions to Accounting Reports
text:
5.1 What report would you design?
An investor asks Campus Curb for its value. A lender asks what resources will be available to repay a loan. Employees ask whether wages can be paid. A founder asks whether a bad result reflects her choices or circumstances beyond her control.
In our ideal model, everyone agreed on the possible cash flows and how to value them. Real reporting involves incomplete evidence, different models, and incentives to influence the depiction. It also has to cover many transactions consistently across entities and periods.
We could ask each user to negotiate a separate report, but doing so is costly. Common reporting conventions help users know what a number represents and compare it with other numbers. Those conventions also constrain some choices a preparer might otherwise make. They cannot make every report equally useful for every purpose.
The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) develops U.S. financial accounting standards. Its conceptual framework states concepts used to develop and evaluate standards. Generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) supply the applicable accounting requirements; the FASB Accounting Standards Codification is the authoritative source of nongovernmental U.S. GAAP, with SEC requirements also relevant to SEC registrants. A concepts statement does not override an applicable standard (Financial Accounting Standards Board 2026).

text:
5.2 What the framework contributes
For business reporting, the framework focuses on information useful to investors, lenders, and other creditors in resource decisions. It includes information about how management discharged its responsibilities. Reports help users estimate an entity’s value; they are not designed to show that value directly.
Information needs relevance and faithful representation. Relevance includes predictive and confirmatory usefulness. Faithful representation concerns completeness, neutrality, and freedom from error in the depiction; it does not demand perfect foresight. Comparability, verifiability, timeliness, and understandability enhance usefulness, subject to a cost constraint (Financial Accounting Standards Board 2024b, OB2–7 and QC5–QC39).
Apply those ideas to a scooter-life estimate. Does the estimate reflect usage evidence? Is the method explained? Has it been applied consistently? Can someone inspect the evidence and reproduce the calculation? Reporting five years because it increases income fails a different test from reporting five years because documented usage supports that estimate.
Avoid a shortcut in which historical cost is always faithful and current value is always relevant. A carefully explained estimate can be faithfully represented; a precisely recorded irrelevant amount can still be unhelpful. The question is what phenomenon the report purports to depict and whether its depiction helps the specified decision.






Assigned framework selections



Use the FASB’s consolidated framework linked in the bibliography. Read OB4 and OB7; QC15–QC18; E16–E17 and E37–E38; RD4–RD7; M5–M8. These short selections address stewardship, valuation, estimates, definitions, recognition, and measurement. Do not read all five chapters for this week.

text:
5.3 Four questions that should not be collapsed into one

Definition: what kind of item is it?
The asset definition concerns an entity’s present right to an economic benefit; the liability definition concerns a present obligation to transfer an economic benefit. Equity is the residual after liabilities. Definitions identify kinds of items rather than a single required measurement (Financial Accounting Standards Board 2021).
An enforceable customer receivable can exist even if collection is uncertain. Uncertainty about the amount ultimately collected does not necessarily erase the present right. Conversely, hoping for future customers does not itself establish a present right to their future payments.


Recognition: should it appear in the statements?
Recognition includes an item in the financial statements. The recognition chapter identifies criteria concerning an element definition, measurability, and faithful representation (Financial Accounting Standards Board 2023, RD4–7). Meeting a definition is not the whole recognition analysis. For an actual transaction, the relevant GAAP requirements determine the treatment.
Ask separately: Does a resource or obligation exist? Does the accounting requirement call for recognition? Treating every useful business attribute as a recognizable asset skips that distinction.


Measurement: what amount, and what subsequent changes?
The framework’s measurement chapter develops entry-price and exit-price systems. Entry-price accounting involves the acquisition or assumption price and subsequent allocations or adjustments; exit-price accounting involves remeasurement. The chapter also distinguishes market-participant and entity-specific perspectives (Financial Accounting Standards Board 2024a, M5–22).
Our prior present-value examples supplied entity cash flows under explicit assumptions. They were not instructions to label every discounted forecast “fair value.” A real measurement needs an identified attribute, perspective, date, and method.


Presentation and disclosure: how will users understand it?
A number in the statements and an explanation in the notes do different jobs. A delivery asset’s carrying amount does not tell users its estimated useful life or how that estimate was chosen. Reporting an estimate without explaining its basis can leave a reader unable to interpret it. Notes supplement the statements; they are not permission to omit an entry required by GAAP.

5.4 A reporting choice for the class
Campus Curb paid $3,600 for scooters. After one month their carrying amount under the supplied cost-allocation policy is $3,500. A documented offer to buy the used scooters is $3,200. The founders estimate $4,200 of discounted net cash flows from continuing to operate them. You have not yet assessed the forecasts’ assumptions or the offer’s terms.
For a hypothetical standard-setting exercise, compare a cost-based report, a report using the proposed sale amount, and a report using the operating forecast. Each group represents an investor, lender, manager-evaluation committee, or preparer. Identify the decision, the attribute measured, supporting evidence, and information still needed. Propose a measurement policy and accompanying note.
This exercise asks what a rule should achieve. It does not claim that the three amounts are interchangeable GAAP choices. In particular, operating value may include resources and activities beyond the scooters themselves, and an offer may not establish a market-participant fair value.
Standards also affect incentives and impose costs. The political-economy perspective associated with Watts and Zimmerman (1978) encourages us to ask who benefits, who bears costs, and who participates in the process. It does not establish that every existing rule is optimal or that every disagreement is regulatory capture.

6.1 An increase can still disappoint
Elm Devices announces earnings per share (EPS) of $1.20. Last year’s comparable EPS was $1.00, but a forecast available before the announcement was $1.40. Earnings increased by $0.20 and fell short of the forecast by $0.20. These comparisons answer different questions. News is the difference between what was learned and what was expected; it is not simply the sign of profit or its change from last year.
The forecast and actual number must use the same accounting definition and share basis. A forecast of adjusted EPS cannot automatically be compared with GAAP EPS. Nor does a forecast necessarily describe every investor’s expectations. In this exercise it is a supplied benchmark, not an observed consensus we have independently verified.
A job candidate might investigate whether disappointing news changes expected hiring or the firm’s ability to pay wages. A lender might investigate cash available for repayment. An investor might revise expected distributions. A report can be useful even when its news is unwelcome, as in Chapter 4.

A stock’s return includes influences shared with other stocks. A market-adjusted abnormal return subtracts the same day’s market return:
\[AR_t=R_{stock,t}-R_{market,t},\qquad CAR[a,b]=\sum_{t=a}^{b}AR_t.\]
CAR is a sum over a specified event window. It is not a price level. Here day 0 is the trading day on which the release becomes public before trading opens; each return is close-to-close for that day. An after-close release would first enter the following trading day’s close-to-close window.

6.4 Efficiency is a benchmark, with qualifications
Fama (1970) distinguishes information sets: past prices in weak-form efficiency, public information in semi-strong efficiency, and public plus private information in strong-form efficiency. The taxonomy is background explained here; the full paper is optional.
The semi-strong benchmark asks whether publicly available information permits systematic abnormal profits after allowing for risk and trading costs. It does not predict that prices never move or that all investors earn the same realized return. A rapid response to genuinely new public information is compatible with efficiency.
An empirical test also needs a model of the return required for risk. An apparent abnormal return might reflect slow information processing, an incomplete risk benchmark, or trading frictions. This joint-hypothesis problem limits what a pattern can establish. One successful trade does not refute efficiency; an announcement response does not prove it.

6.5 Ball and Brown: what the historical picture measures
Ball and Brown (1968) examine 261 firms over fiscal years 1957–1965. Their regression news benchmark relates a firm’s annual income change to the market-wide annual income change using firm-specific estimated relationships. It is not an analyst forecast or a cross-sectional median split. Their alternative naive benchmark uses the prior year’s income, but our lab uses the regression-model net-income groups. Estimation details are optional; the contemporaneous market-income input and eventual earnings realization mean this is not a forecast portfolio known a year in advance.
Their return analysis uses monthly, not daily, observations. The abnormal-performance index (API) averages firm-level compounded monthly residual-return paths, starting at 1 before month −11. It is a different statistic from our summed three-day CAR. Month 0 is the annual-announcement month.

7.1 From the December case to an operating-cash reconciliation
In Section 5.5, earning revenue, collecting cash, consuming resources, and paying suppliers could occur at different dates. Those timing differences do not disappear when an organization grows. A customer receivable records a claim from a sale; a payable records an obligation to a supplier. Not every accrual is a forecast of an unobservable amount. Some arise from ordinary contractual timing, while allowances and useful lives require estimates.
Harbor Learning reports net income of 80,000. Its operating balances change as shown below; there are no acquisitions, currency effects, or other reconciling items. The indirect method starts with income and removes the effects that differ from operating cash receipts and payments.
Here CFO = 80,000 and net accruals = income − CFO = 0. Zero net accruals do not mean zero accrual components. Several adjustments offset. CFO also does not prove every sale was collected: the increase in receivables says otherwise. Cash collected for next year’s courses brings an obligation to teach them.
For these simplified balances, an increase in a prepaid operating expense subtracts from income in the CFO reconciliation; a decrease adds back. Explain the payment and consumption dates rather than memorizing a sign without a reason.
The cash-flow statement also separates investing cash, such as equipment purchases and sale proceeds, from financing cash, such as borrowing, issuing shares, and paying dividends. In the U.S. GAAP classification used in our drills, interest paid is operating. Noncash transactions require separate attention; recording depreciation is not another cash purchase of the machine.

7.2 Receivables: estimate first, then write off
Suppose gross customer receivables are 10,000 and the supplied estimate of uncollectible amounts is 4%. The required allowance is 400. Because the allowance already has a 100 credit balance, record only 300 additional expense: Dr Bad debt expense 300; Cr Allowance 300. Net receivables are 10,000 − 400 = 9,600. Next, write off a particular 200 account: Dr Allowance 200; Cr Receivables 200. Gross receivables become 9,800 and the allowance becomes 200, so net receivables remain 9,600. The earlier estimate recognized the loss; this write-off uses the allowance. This is a supplied-percentage teaching case, not a complete expected-credit-loss estimation model.

7.4 An identity does not estimate persistence
Define accruals for our classroom case as net income minus reported CFO. Then
\[Income=CFO+Accruals.\]
This is true by construction. A forecast of next year’s income is a different claim requiring evidence or supplied assumptions. Recall Dechow (1994): accrual accounting can help measure performance when cash timing obscures economic activity. That usefulness is compatible with accrual and cash components having different average persistence in a sample.
Two invented firms each have income 100 and average assets 1,000. A has CFO 80 and accruals 20; B has CFO 20 and accruals 80. Use the illustrative rule
\[\widehat{Income}_{t+1}/Assets=0.010+0.85(CFO_t/Assets)+0.75(Accruals_t/Assets).\]
For A: .010 + .85(.08) + .75(.02) = .093. For B: .010 + .85(.02) + .75(.08) = .087. With next year’s denominator held at 1,000, those are forecasts of 93 and 87. Equal slopes of .80 instead produce 90 for both. The identity did not choose the slopes; different assumptions change the forecast difference.
Collecting last year’s receivable creates cash this year without new revenue. That is a timing example. It cannot by itself demonstrate which earnings component predicts future earnings better across continuing businesses.

7.5 Sloan: definitions before coefficients
Sloan (1996) studies 40,679 firm-years over 1962–1991. The paper’s earnings measure is operating income after depreciation, Compustat item 178, described in its continuing-operations framework; it excludes items such as taxes and nonoperating income. Do not substitute ordinary bottom-line net income merely because both measures are called earnings.
The original accrual calculation is the change in noncash current assets, less the change in current liabilities excluding short-term debt and taxes payable, less depreciation/amortization. Its cash component is earnings minus that measure. Variables are scaled by average total assets. This historical balance-sheet construction and today’s reported CFO decomposition need not agree, especially when acquisitions or other nonoperating balance changes intervene.
Table 3 Panel A’s pooled prediction has intercept .011, accrual slope .765, and cash-flow slope .855. Replacing .01 of scaled accruals with .01 of scaled cash flows, holding current earnings fixed, increases fitted future earnings by (.855 − .765)(.01) = .0009 of assets, or 0.09 percentage points. The table reports a test of slope equality; students read that reported comparison, not estimate a regression. Demand changes, measurement differences, or unusual events can make any firm’s outcome differ from the fit. A large accrual is not an individual fraud diagnosis.

7.6 Future returns are a separate question
Sloan’s Table 6 reports year-t+1 size-adjusted portfolio returns of .049 for the lowest accrual decile and −.055 for the highest: a 10.4-percentage-point historical spread. The intermediate series is not strictly decreasing. Returns subtract a size-matched buy-and-hold benchmark and include distributions; measurement begins four months after fiscal year-end. That delay addresses information availability, but a modern test still needs actual release dates.
The paper’s uncertainty calculation uses annual portfolio returns. Ten published decile averages are not ten independent observations for a fresh t-test. Persistence differences alone do not imply unexploited returns: investors may already understand them. Risk benchmarks, costs, availability, and a new sample can alter the conclusion. text:
8.1 What amount helps which decision?
An asset is a present right to an economic benefit; recognition and measurement require additional analysis under the applicable standard. Spending money is not sufficient proof that a valuable asset exists. Nor does the absence of a recognized asset establish that the activity has no future benefit.
Useful reporting needs both relevance and faithful representation, as discussed in Chapter 5. Historical cost does not own faithful representation, and fair value does not own relevance. A purchase invoice can be verifiable while accumulated cost poorly answers today’s resale question. A well-supported fair-value estimate can faithfully represent a relevant current measurement even though it is uncertain. Choosing a basis, estimating its inputs, and checking the evidence are distinct tasks.
A donor deciding whether to fund replacement equipment and a lender estimating collateral proceeds may need different information. Ask what the recorded amount measures and what further evidence the decision needs.

section: 8.2 Equipment: cost and allocation
text:
8.2 Equipment: cost and allocation
A community training center pays 12,000 for a machine, 1,000 for delivery, and 2,000 for installation. It also prepays 1,200 for next year’s insurance. Under the case assumptions, equipment cost is 15,000; insurance is a separate prepaid asset, expensed as coverage is consumed. It is not part of equipment cost.
The machine is ready for use immediately and has a four-year useful life and 3,000 residual value. Straight-line depreciation allocates the depreciable amount over the service period:
\[Annual\ depreciation=(15,000-3,000)/4=3,000.\]
Record Dr Depreciation expense 3,000; Cr Accumulated depreciation 3,000. The credit is a contra-asset, leaving original equipment cost visible. Cash does not change at this entry. After two full years the carrying amount is 15,000 − 6,000 = 9,000. Depreciation allocates cost; it does not estimate a new resale price every year.
For partial years, apply the stated convention. An asset ready for use October 1 with full-year depreciation of 6,000 has three months’ depreciation of 1,500 through December 31 under our monthly convention. Acquisition and readiness dates need not coincide in real cases.

section: 8.3 Disposal and impairment answer different questions
text:
8.3 Disposal and impairment answer different questions
If the machine is sold after Year 2 for 8,000, proceeds are 1,000 below its 9,000 carrying amount. Record Dr Cash 8,000; Dr Accumulated depreciation 6,000; Dr Loss 1,000; Cr Equipment 15,000. Remove both original cost and accumulated depreciation. Comparing proceeds with original cost would overstate the loss.
Now consider a separate alternative: the center keeps the machine, and an impairment review is warranted. Treat it as the entire relevant held-and-used asset group for this simplified ASC 360 exercise. Remaining undiscounted cash flows are 8,500 and fair value is 7,000. Apply the supplied two-step rule:

Recoverability screen: carrying amount 9,000 exceeds undiscounted cash flows 8,500.
Loss measurement: write down to fair value 7,000, recognizing a 2,000 loss.

The 500 shortfall at the first step is not the measured loss. If undiscounted cash flows instead were 9,500, this screen would not trigger a loss, even with fair value below carrying amount. This held-and-used rule does not apply universally to goodwill, inventory, or assets held for sale. Real application requires the appropriate grouping and supported cash-flow estimates; the exercise supplies both. SEC correspondence discussing ASC 360’s cash-flow screen.
The board should request evidence on condition, utilization, demand, maintenance, and replacement plans. “Management estimates it” is the start of the investigation, not its end.

9.1 An obligation and the incentives around it
A liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic benefit. Borrowing creates a repayment claim, even if management would prefer to use the cash elsewhere. Shareholders can benefit from risky projects or distributions while creditors bear part of the downside. Contracts can limit those choices, require information, and specify when creditors gain additional rights.
An accounting amount is therefore useful both as information and as an input into an agreement. A lender may define “debt” or “earnings” differently from a financial-statement subtotal. Before calculating a covenant ratio, read its numerator, denominator, testing date, threshold, and remedies. A ratio rank among other firms supplies none of those terms.

9.4 Contract A and Contract B: the same firm, different compliance
The firm has bank loans 70, bonds 20, lease liabilities 10, EBITDA before permitted adjustments 24, and stock compensation 6, all in millions. EBITDA is an earnings subtotal before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization; adjusted EBITDA depends on which further adjustments a contract permits. Neither is automatically cash available to pay debt.
Contract A tests funded debt divided by trailing-twelve-month adjusted EBITDA at quarter-end, with a maximum of 3.50. Funded debt includes bank loans and bonds but excludes leases. Adjusted EBITDA adds stock compensation to the supplied 24 and permits no other add-backs. There are no waivers or cure rights in this numerical case.
Debt = 70 + 20 = 90; adjusted EBITDA = 24 + 6 = 30; ratio = 3.00. Define upper-limit ratio slack as maximum minus actual: 3.50 − 3.00 = +0.50, so the firm complies. Its debt headroom at fixed EBITDA is 3.50(30) − 90 = 15 million, a different unit from ratio slack.
Contract B includes leases and prohibits the stock-compensation add-back, with the same limit. The ratio is 100/24 = 4.17 and slack is approximately −0.67: a violation under the supplied terms. Identical financial statements have produced different contractual conclusions.
For a minimum interest-coverage test, reverse the subtraction: actual minus minimum. If defined EBIT is 4.8 million, defined interest is 1.2 million, and the minimum is 3.0, actual coverage is 4.0 and slack is +1.0. Define the sign before interpreting it.

(Interest-coverage covenant.) A firm has EBIT of $4,800,000 and interest expense of $1,200,000. The contract defines coverage as the supplied EBIT divided by the supplied interest expense and requires coverage of at least 3.0×. Compute the ratio and the covenant slack.
(Debt-to-EBITDA covenant.) Use these amounts as the contractually defined numerator and denominator, with no other adjustments. A firm has total debt of $90 million and EBITDA of $30 million. A covenant caps debt-to-EBITDA at 3.5×. Compute the ratio and state whether the covenant is satisfied.

Premium or discount? Discount — the coupon (6%) is below the market rate (8%), so investors will pay less than face. Interest expense will be greater than the cash coupon, because expense is the carrying amount times the 8% market rate.
Issue price. Present value at 8%: coupons = 6,000 × annuity factor (2.577097) = $15,463; face = 100,000 × PV factor (0.793832) = $79,383. Issue price ≈ $94,846 (a $5,154 discount).
Effective-interest amortization. Year-1 interest expense = 94,846 × 8% = $7,588. Cash coupon = $6,000, so discount amortized = 7,588 − 6,000 = $1,588. Carrying value end of year 1 = 94,846 + 1,588 = $96,434.
Issuance entry (gross method). Dr Cash $94,846; Dr Discount on Bonds Payable $5,154; Cr Bonds Payable $100,000.
Bond at par. (a) Dr Cash $200,000; Cr Bonds Payable $200,000. (b) Dr Interest Expense $10,000 (200,000 × 5%); Cr Cash $10,000.
Lease liability. PV of $10,000 for four years at 6% = 10,000 × annuity factor (3.4651) = $34,651.
Optional — Lease classification. (a) ownership transfer points to finance classification; (b) a nine-month term alone does not establish or exclude finance classification, and the full contract and any short-term election matter; (c) 90% points to a major part of economic life; (d) 97% points to substantially all of fair value. Interest coverage. Ratio = 4,800,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 4.0×. Slack = 4.0 − 3.0 = 1.0× (in compliance).
Debt-to-EBITDA. Ratio = 90 ÷ 30 = 3.0×. Since 3.0× ≤ 3.5×, the covenant is satisfied (slack of 0.5×).

10.4 A threshold can reward changing the number or the activity
Return to the firm with income of 100,000 after equity compensation. A separate cash bonus of 2,000 is earned if net income before this cash bonus but after equity compensation reaches 105,000. That definition avoids a circular threshold calculation.
The manager proposes reducing an otherwise supported warranty expense estimate by 6,000. Before the cash bonus, income would become 106,000, crossing the threshold. If the bonus is then recognized, final income is 104,000. Changing an expense estimate does not itself create cash. Ask whether new product-quality, repair-cost, or claims evidence justifies the reduction independently of the bonus. An incentive to change an estimate does not establish that any particular revision is false.
As a separate alternative, cancel 6,000 of employee training that otherwise would be expensed and paid this year. Income before the cash bonus again becomes 106,000. This changes a real activity and preserves 6,000 cash before the bonus payment. If the 2,000 bonus is paid now, the net current cash improvement is 4,000. Future service quality or employee retention may suffer. A decision can improve this year’s accounting metric without improving the organization’s long-run outcome.

title: 11  Decentralization and Cost Behavior
text:
11.1 Who should decide?
Imagine a service network for Tesla or Rivian with three locations. This is a constructed organizational case, not a description of either company’s actual delegation policy. A local manager knows service queues, staffing, and parts delays; headquarters sees capital needs and purchasing opportunities across locations. Who should set service hours, approve suppliers, and authorize a new facility?
Hayek (1945) emphasizes knowledge of particular circumstances held by people close to the activity. Moving every decision to the center can discard that information or require costly communication. Delegation lets the local manager act on it. Delegation also gives someone with their own preferences discretion over the organization’s resources. A manager might prefer convenient hours, an oversized staff or a project that expands their role.
The choice depends on both information and incentives. Let a local manager adapt opening hours within a budget, coordinate repair-quality procedures across locations, and have the center evaluate a large capital investment using local forecasts and independent evidence. No single organizational level must own every decision. The same reasoning applies to charities, hospital departments and university colleges.
Internal accounting helps the manager choose and helps others evaluate that choice. These uses can conflict. A cost allocated for performance reporting need not be avoidable when making a particular decision.

11.3 Cost behavior within a stated range
A variable cost changes in total with activity. A fixed cost remains unchanged in total over the specified activity range and horizon. Fixed cost per unit falls as volume rises; that does not make total cost variable. A mixed cost contains both components. Room rental can be fixed for one semester and avoidable when the contract expires. An additional supervisor can create a step when activity exceeds capacity.
For our constructed examples assume one product, constant price and variable cost per unit, unchanged total fixed cost, adequate capacity, and production equal to sales. Test these assumptions before applying the model to a real organization.
Let price be P, variable cost per unit V, quantity Q and fixed cost F:
\[CM\ per\ unit=P-V;\qquad Operating\ income=Q(P-V)-F.\]
Contribution margin pays for fixed costs and then contributes to operating income. It is not gross profit: financial-statement cost of goods sold need not equal variable cost.

11.7 What cost information can establish
Rivian’s fiscal 2025 Form 10-K reports revenue of $5.387 billion, gross profit of $0.144 billion, and an operating loss of $3.585 billion. Its 2024 comparative figures are revenue $4.970 billion, gross loss $1.200 billion, and operating loss $4.689 billion. Gross profit improves by $1.344 billion, but it is neither operating profit nor contribution margin. Rivian 2025 Form 10-K, printed p. 75.
Use the festival model to learn the calculation, then ask which assumptions a Rivian or Tesla application needs. The reported totals do not identify variable cost per vehicle or fixed cost. Changes in mix, prices, production and other circumstances can affect the comparison. Do not label assumed costs as observed 10-K data or interpret the revenue/profit association as a causal estimate of operating leverage.
Self-check. Why does fixed cost per attendee fall from 15 at break-even to about 10.91 at 11,000 attendees? The same 120,000 commitment is divided among more attendees. The decrease in the average does not itself save cash.

text:
11.9 Optional extension: transfer prices and richer costs
A transfer price assigns revenue and cost to divisions trading internally. With spare capacity, no displaced sale and incremental cost $40, a transfer can be worthwhile when the receiving division’s incremental benefit exceeds $40. If supplying internally displaces an outside sale, include the lost contribution as opportunity cost. A market price is not automatically the marginal cost of an internal transfer. Variable-cost pricing can give the buyer a useful marginal signal while leaving the seller needing another way to recover capacity costs; full-cost pricing can affect sourcing incentives. Internal evaluation and tax transfer-pricing compliance are separate design questions.
High-low estimation, margin of safety, activity-based costing and cost stickiness are optional extensions. They are not required for Quiz 4 or the final. The next chapter asks how a report changes choices even when the arithmetic is correct.

title: 12  Performance Measurement as Agency
text:
12.1 A report rewards some activities more than others
A manager wants staff to solve customers’ problems. A count of completed calls is cheap to collect. Paying for completed calls may encourage faster service; it may also reward ending difficult calls too soon. The count and the organization’s objective differ.
Holmstrom and Milgrom (1991) studies incentives when agents perform several tasks and performance is measured unevenly. When tasks compete for effort, stronger rewards for one measured task can divert effort from another valuable task. Lower-powered rewards can then be useful. The conclusion depends on task substitution, costs, measurement and the other incentives workers face. It is not a universal instruction to eliminate bonuses or reject better monitoring.

12.3 Wells Fargo: apply the mechanism to evidence
In September 2016 the CFPB reported unauthorized account practices at Wells Fargo and linked them to sales goals and compensation incentives. The action required refunds and a $100 million CFPB penalty; contemporaneous combined fines from the CFPB, OCC and Los Angeles totaled $185 million. These are historical enforcement findings, not a controlled comparison of incentive systems. CFPB action summary and September 8, 2016 remarks.
Identify the rewarded measure, the customer outcome it could miss, behavior that changes the measure, and controls that could detect it. Reducing pressure on account counts, checking customer authorization independently and protecting escalation channels address different parts of the problem. Evaluate the benefit and cost of each. Do not assert that a particular reform would certainly have prevented every violation.
In class, write your diagnosis and two proposed reforms before AI. Then critique an AI answer or a supplied printed answer. Credit a sound answer when it is sound. Better measurement is not automatically inconsistent with multitasking theory.

section: 12.4 ROI and residual income use a specified accounting basis
text:
12.4 ROI and residual income use a specified accounting basis
For required cases, taxes are ignored, operating profit and average operating assets are supplied, and the required return is on that same stated basis:
\[ROI=\frac{Operating\ profit}{Average\ operating\ assets};\qquad RI=Operating\ profit-r(Average\ operating\ assets).\]
A division earns $40 million on average operating assets of $200 million. The supplied capital charge is 10%. ROI is 20% and RI is 20 million. A project adds profit $7 million and average operating assets $50 million. Its accounting return is 14%. After acceptance, division ROI becomes 47/250 = 18.8%; RI becomes 47−.10(250) = 22 million.
If paid solely to raise this year’s ROI, the manager sees a lower rewarded metric. If paid solely to raise RI, the project adds 2 million. These are predictions under the stated contract; career concerns, future rewards and nonfinancial goals can change behavior.
The calculation does not alone establish NPV. To connect the two, supply a cash-flow model. Suppose the project pays 7 million cash at year-end, returns its entire 50 million investment then, and has no other cash flows. Average operating assets are defined as 50 million for the full operating period; no depreciation is needed because capital is fully recovered. NPV = −50 + 57/1.10 = 1.818 million. In this deliberately specified one-period case, positive RI and NPV recommendations agree. For a depreciating multi-year asset, use the full timeline; one year’s accounting return is insufficient.
RI is in dollars and ROI is a rate. A large division can earn more RI with a lower ROI than a small division. Compare opportunities and changes within context rather than rank manager ability from either number alone. Asset age, measurement policies and controllability affect both.

(Labor efficiency variance.) The standard is 2 hours per unit at $20.00 per hour; 2,000 units are produced; actual hours total 4,200. Compute the direct-labor efficiency variance.
(Return on investment.) A division reports operating income of $600,000 and average operating assets of $3,000,000. Compute ROI.
(Residual income.) For the same division (operating income $600,000; operating assets $3,000,000), the required rate of return is 14%. Compute residual income.
(Economic value added.) A firm has NOPAT of $1,200,000, invested capital of $8,000,000, and a weighted-average cost of capital of 10%. Compute EVA.

Materials price variance. = (actual price − standard price) × actual quantity = (5.30 − 5.00) × 8,000 = $2,400 U.

section: 12.8 Optional extension: EVA and formal models
text:
12.8 Optional extension: EVA and formal models
An EVA-style measure subtracts a capital charge from adjusted net operating profit after tax (NOPAT), using invested capital and a compatible weighted-average cost of capital. RI does not intrinsically require cost of equity: the required return must match the profit and capital basis. Do not improve a comparison merely by choosing a lower rate.
For a supplied adjustment, begin with NOPAT 100 and invested capital 500, in millions; WACC is 10%. Unadjusted residual operating profit is 50. Suppose after-tax current R&D expense is 20, amortization would be 12, and the supplied average unamortized R&D capital is 60. Adjusted NOPAT is 100+20−12 = 108; adjusted capital is 560; the measure is 108−.10(560) = 52. This is sensitivity to an accounting model, not a discovered market value. Do not add operating leases again if already included in the capital base.
Labor variances apply analogous rate/efficiency decompositions. The formal Holmstrom–Milgrom model and Chapter 4’s optional LEN derivation deepen the incentive conditions. These extensions are excluded from Quiz 4 and the final.






Holmstrom, Bengt, and Paul Milgrom. 1991. “Multitask Principal-Agent Analyses: Incentive Contracts, Asset Ownership, and Job Design.” Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization 7: 24–52.

title: 13  Capital Budgeting Under Asymmetric Information
text:
13.1 Start with incremental cash flows
A machine may make a department’s reported profit larger while destroying value. A worthwhile investment may lower its short-term ROI. Evaluate the cash flows that change when the organization accepts the project, including the timing of costs, benefits and any recovery at the end.
For a constructed example, pay 100 now to receive 60 at the end of each of the next two years. The supplied discount rate is 10%; these are incremental after-tax cash flows with no other outlays or terminal proceeds.
\[NPV=-100+\frac{60}{1.10}+\frac{60}{1.10^2}=4.132.\]
The 100 is paid now and is not discounted. The first 60 has PV 54.545; the second has PV 49.587. Positive NPV means the project adds value under these cash-flow and discount-rate assumptions. Do not subtract depreciation as a second cash outlay when the equipment payment is already included. If taxes matter, their cash effects must be included; this course supplies them or explicitly ignores taxes.
A sunk cost paid before today’s decision is not changed by that decision. The cash from selling an existing asset instead of using it is an opportunity cost. Working capital tied up initially and recovered at the end belongs in the timeline. State what is included, not merely a formula.

13.3 Flexibility belongs inside the valuation
A rigid plan and a contingent plan must use the same states and payoffs if their difference is to measure flexibility. Consider a two-stage project, amounts in millions. Assume risk neutrality, a 10% discount rate, and no cash flows beyond those specified.
Pay 4 now to learn at time 1 whether demand is strong or weak, each with probability .5. Commercialization at time 1 costs 8. Its cash payoff at time 2 is 16 in the strong state and 4 in the weak state.
At time 1, commercialization NPV is −8+16/1.10 = 6.545 if strong and −8+4/1.10 = −4.364 if weak. A flexible manager commercializes only if strong.








Policy after paying for research
Value at time 0




Must commercialize in either state
−4 − 8/1.10 + [.5(16)+.5(4)]/1.10² = −3.008


May decline commercialization after seeing demand
−4 + .5[−8+16/1.10]/1.10 = −1.025




The option to decline adds 1.983 million, the present value of avoiding the weak-state loss. Both policies still have negative initial NPV, so the firm should decline the research investment if these are the only benefits. Valuable flexibility does not guarantee a valuable overall project.
NPV is capable of valuing this contingent policy. A calculation that already conditions the follow-on cost on success already includes that flexibility; do not add it again. Uncertainty alone is not option value. Value comes from a useful future choice informed by what is learned.

section: 13.4 Information changes the allocation problem
text:
13.4 Information changes the allocation problem
The center cannot evaluate projects well if managers have private information and gain from obtaining capital regardless of value. Antle and Eppen (1985) models a relationship among private information, organizational slack, rationing and cutoff rates above market rates. This establishes possibilities under a model’s assumptions, not a universal instruction to cut every request by 20%. Publisher abstract.
The in-class allocation game uses indivisible one-period projects, a fixed budget and privately known terminal cash. Terminal cash includes recovery of the investment. A project’s value is:
\[NPV=-Investment+\frac{Terminal\ cash}{1.10}.\]
For investment 40 and terminal cash 48, NPV is 3.636, not 48−.10(40). If accounting profit were 8 and average capital 40 on a compatible one-period basis, RI would be 4; discounted RI is 4/1.10 = 3.636. These quantities have different timing and names.
Managers in the game earn a bonus for funded capital; headquarters scores total NPV. The bonus therefore creates a reason to request funds even for a negative-NPV project. Headquarters must consider evidence and its verification cost. In a second round, one independently checked claim provides information before allocation. Compare outcomes with the feasible optimum, but do not interpret a few classroom rounds as an equilibrium estimate or a causal test of a general theory.
Self-check. With budget 60, indivisible project A costs 40 and has NPV 8; B costs 30 with NPV 7; C costs 30 with NPV 7. Fund B+C, NPV 14, rather than A alone. Ranking individual projects by absolute NPV misses the combination constraint.

section: 13.6 Optional extension: IRR and profitability index
text:
13.6 Optional extension: IRR and profitability index
IRR is a discount rate at which NPV equals zero. With one initial outflow followed only by positive inflows, a unique positive IRR, when it exists, can be compared with the compatible required return. The extended example’s IRR is 17.178948%. For mutually exclusive projects, dollar NPV at the appropriate rate governs value; a smaller project can have a higher IRR but less NPV.
Multiple sign changes permit multiple IRRs but do not ensure them. Cash flows −100, 230, −132 have IRRs 10% and 20%. In contrast, −100, 400, −400 has NPV = −100(r−1)²/(1+r)² and only one distinct IRR, 100%, a repeated root. Use the NPV at the required rate to avoid interpreting an arbitrary solver root as a decision rule.
Profitability index is PV of future inflows divided by initial cost, or 1+NPV/cost for this simple structure. Under special divisible-project assumptions it can help allocate a limited budget. With indivisible projects, check feasible combinations. Formal option pricing, IRR solving, PI optimization, influence-cost models and the empirical diversification literature are optional, outside the final’s required scope.






Antle, Rick, and Gary D. Eppen. 1985. “Capital Rationing and Organizational Slack in Capital Budgeting.” Management Science 31 (2): 163–74.


Graham, John R., and Campbell R. Harvey. 2001. “The Theory and Practice of Corporate Finance: Evidence from the Field.” Journal of Financial Economics 60 (2–3): 187–243.

Read this chapter and the short common brief for the debate you are preparing. No full paper or optional technical extension becomes required because it appears in a bibliography. The four debates occur April 20, April 22, April 27 and April 29, 2027.
The course began with a user making a decision. Certainty linked cash flows to value; uncertainty and private information made that link harder. Accrual accounting addressed timing and measurement. Market evidence asked what reported numbers reveal. Internal accounting showed that reports also change choices. The debates bring those functions together.
For each claim, distinguish a model prediction, an observed association, a constructed example and a causal conclusion. The absence of a cash payment does not mean the absence of an economic cost. A numerical estimate does not remove uncertainty. A disclosure can both reveal information and change incentives.

14.3 Debate 1: mandatory climate-related disclosure
April 20. Resolved: A mandatory, standardized climate-related financial disclosure regime would improve capital allocation enough to justify its compliance costs.
Consider economically material risks to the reporting organization, usable measurement, enforcement and burdens on firms of different sizes. The affirmative should explain how information changes a decision. The negative should compare the proposed regime with a feasible alternative, including costs of missing or inconsistent information.
This is a policy comparison, not a claim that a particular current rule has already produced measured benefits. The SEC adopted climate-disclosure rules in 2024, stayed them during litigation and proposed rescinding them in May 2026. A proposal to rescind is not a completed rescission. The dated institutional note must be rechecked before the debate. SEC May 29, 2026 fact sheet.
The common brief supplies a constructed benefit/cost comparison. It cannot establish the effect of an actual rule. IFRS-adoption findings or stock-price associations are not direct experiments on the proposed climate policy.

14.4 Debate 2: goodwill measurement
April 22. Resolved: For a public company, acquired goodwill should be remeasured annually with both upward and downward changes recognized in income, instead of the current impairment model.
For this hypothetical proposal, remeasure only the acquired-goodwill component using an explicitly documented allocation of reporting-unit value; do not recognize new internally generated goodwill separately. This restriction does not solve the difficult problem of separating the acquired component from subsequently created value. Teams must address it.
The required baseline is the public-company impairment model discussed in Chapter 8: goodwill is not routinely amortized, and impairment assessment occurs annually and between annual tests when qualifying circumstances arise. Eligible private-company/not-for-profit alternatives are outside this resolution. Annual impairment testing is not the same as unrestricted annual upward/downward remeasurement. FASB ASU 2017-04.
Compare delayed recognition with estimation uncertainty, managerial discretion, verification cost and implications for contracts. Do not promise that a fair-value estimate removes discretion or that an impairment-only carrying amount is an observable current value.

14.5 Debate 3: share-based compensation and performance measures
April 27. Resolved: A board should exclude expense for equity-classified employee service awards from its primary annual operating-performance measure.
Use the simple service awards from Chapter 10: grant-date value is supplied, service is recognized over the specified period, and no forfeiture, modification, tax or diluted-EPS complication is required. The proposal changes the board’s internal primary performance measure, not GAAP recognition.
Both sides must acknowledge that employee services have a cost even when payment is in shares. The affirmative can argue that a particular annual measure should separate compensation policy from operating execution, but must explain how the board will still hold decision-makers accountable for the cost. The negative can argue that exclusion rewards substitution toward stock pay or obscures resource use, but must consider whether supplementary measures address a real comparison problem. Assess a reconciled GAAP-to-adjusted measure and the incentives it creates.
This replaces the earlier tax-deductibility resolution. No tax-law or option-pricing prerequisite is added.

14.6 Debate 4: hidden characteristics and hidden actions
April 29. Resolved: The principal benefit of mandatory sustainability reporting is improved accountability for hidden actions, rather than better information about hidden characteristics.
Moral hazard is a form of information asymmetry. The distinction here is hidden action versus hidden characteristics, not moral hazard versus information. A report can affect both. Specify a setting, a stakeholder and an outcome before arguing which mechanism is primary.
For example, emissions information might help a lender distinguish otherwise similar borrowers and might also help a board evaluate a manager’s subsequent choices. External harm is not automatically hidden action: an observable externality can still motivate policy. Reporting alone may not change behavior unless users can act on what is learned.

14.7 Classroom format and preparation
The instructor randomly assigns eight speaking teams, two per debate, separately from project groups. Each student belongs to one speaking team and contributes to its argument; other students serve as the audience on that date. Three audience members provide advisory evaluations. Publish the team roster and positions by March 30 so preparation time is equal.
Each team sends its constructive argument to the instructor and opponent 48 hours before its debate, as the syllabus requires. At a 9:05 a.m. class time, deadlines are April 18, April 20, April 25 and April 27 at 9:05 a.m. Eastern. Begin with independent reasoning; follow the syllabus’s debate-specific AI rules. There is no additional late-unit individual essay.
The first three meetings use a 60-minute debate: two 8-minute constructives, two 4-minute cross-examinations, two 5-minute rebuttals, two 3-minute conclusions, and 20 minutes of audience questions. Add a 5-minute opening, 7-minute evidence debrief and 3-minute exit note for a 75-minute meeting.
The final debate uses 45 minutes: two 6-minute constructives, two 3-minute cross-examinations, two 4-minute rebuttals, two 2-minute conclusions, and 15 minutes of audience questions. Add a 5-minute opening, 5-minute evidence debrief and 20-minute retrospective.

B.4 Querying WRDS
The simplest way to pull data from WRDS is db.raw_sql(...), which executes an arbitrary SQL query against the WRDS PostgreSQL database and returns a pandas DataFrame. For example:
df = db.raw_sql("""
    SELECT gvkey, datadate, fyear, at, ib
    FROM comp.funda
    WHERE indfmt = 'INDL'
      AND datafmt = 'STD'
      AND fyear BETWEEN 2018 AND 2024
""", date_cols=['datadate'])
The date_cols argument tells pandas to parse the named columns as dates rather than strings.

B.6 Common pitfalls

Linking CRSP to Compustat. Use crsp.ccmxpf_lnkhist (the CRSP/Compustat Merged linking table). Filter on linktype IN ('LU','LC') and linkprim IN ('P','C').
Adjusting for splits. CRSP daily returns are already split-adjusted; CRSP daily prices are not.
Trading days vs. calendar days. Use crsp.dsi as your trading-day calendar; do not infer trading days from crsp.dsf alone.
Earnings announcement dates. Compustat’s rdq (on comp.fundq) is the date the firm announced; it is not always the date the market reacted to the announcement, especially for after-hours announcements.
Pickling intermediate DataFrames. Free Colab sessions disconnect after about 90 minutes of inactivity, and the WRDS pulls in the larger labs take several minutes each. Mount your Google Drive (drive.mount('/content/drive')) and save intermediate DataFrames to a folder there using df.to_pickle(...). You can then reload them in subsequent sessions without re-running the queries.
pip install is per-session. Colab does not persist installed packages across sessions. The !pip install wrds --quiet cell must run every time you reopen the notebook.

section: C.3 What equal debits and credits prove
text:
C.3 What equal debits and credits prove
Equal totals establish a form of internal consistency. They do not prove that a reported receivable exists, that an estimate is appropriate, or that all obligations were recorded. A fictitious receivable and revenue can balance. Evidence and controls address questions the bookkeeping identity cannot answer.

D.12 Chapter 11: Gross profit is not contribution margin
Rivian moves from a gross loss of 1,200 in 2024 to gross profit of 144 in 2025 while reporting operating losses in both years. Compute the gross-profit change and reconcile 2025 gross profit to operating loss using operating expenses of 3,729. Source: Rivian Form 10-K, printed p. 75.
Self-check: gross profit improves by 1,344; 144 minus 3,729 equals (3,585). Neither gross profit nor two years of revenue and operating income supplies the fixed/variable cost split needed for contribution-margin analysis.
